[...] The easiest way to see this is to stop thinking about copper as supply and start thinking about copper as movement. Production data alone gives a misleading sense of stability. The United States produces just over 1.1 million tonnes annually, Canada contributes roughly 0.5 million tonnes, and at first glance, that suggests a region with meaningful supply capacity. But once you follow the material, the structure looks very different. In 2023, the U.S. still imported approximately 890,000 tonnes of refined copper, while Canada exported around 450,000 tonnes of concentrate, most of it to Asia for processing. This means the system is not self-contained; it is dependent on long-distance logistics and external refining capacity. Copper is mined in one place, processed in another, and consumed in a third. snippet: What makes the current copper setup so interesting is not that the market is wrong, but that it is incomplete in a very specific way. Most participants already understand that demand is going higher, and in fact, that part of the thesis has become consensus. You hear the same numbers repeated across desks: roughly 25 million tonnes of annual demand today, moving toward 35–40 million tonnes over the next decade, driven by electrification, AI infrastructure, renewable energy, and increasingly electrified defense systems. There is no edge in restating those drivers. The edge sits in recognizing that these forecasts assume a system that behaves more smoothly than the real one does. Because copper does not exist as a number — it exists as a chain of physical processes, and those processes do not scale linearly. They stretch, they delay, and eventually, they bottleneck. [...] The easiest way to see this is to stop thinking about copper as supply and start thinking about copper as movement. Production data alone gives a misleading sense of stability. The United States produces just over 1.1 million tonnes annually, Canada contributes roughly 0.5 million tonnes, and at first glance, that suggests a region with meaningful supply capacity. But once you follow the material, the structure looks very different. In 2023, the U.S. still imported approximately 890,000 tonnes of refined copper, while Canada exported around 450,000 tonnes of concentrate, most of it to Asia for processing. This means the system is not self-contained; it is dependent on long-distance logistics and external refining capacity. Copper is mined in one place, processed in another, and consumed in a third. snippet: What makes the current copper setup so interesting is not that the market is wrong, but that it is incomplete in a very specific way. Most participants already understand that demand is going higher, and in fact, that part of the thesis has become consensus. You hear the same numbers repeated across desks: roughly 25 million tonnes of annual demand today, moving toward 35–40 million tonnes over the next decade, driven by electrification, AI infrastructure, renewable energy, and increasingly electrified defense systems. There is no edge in restating those drivers. The edge sits in recognizing that these forecasts assume a system that behaves more smoothly than the real one does. Because copper does not exist as a number — it exists as a chain of physical processes, and those processes do not scale linearly. They stretch, they delay, and eventually, they bottleneck. [...] The easiest way to see this is to stop thinking about copper as supply and start thinking about copper as movement. Production data alone gives a misleading sense of stability. The United States produces just over 1.1 million tonnes annually, Canada contributes roughly 0.5 million tonnes, and at first glance, that suggests a region with meaningful supply capacity. snippet: What makes the current copper setup so interesting is not that the market is wrong, but that it is incomplete in a very specific way. Most participants already understand that demand is going higher, and in fact, that part of the thesis has become consensus. You hear the same numbers repeated across desks: roughly 25 million tonnes of annual demand today, moving toward 35–40 million tonnes over the next decade, driven by electrification, AI infrastructure, renewable energy, and increasingly electrified defense systems. There is no edge in restating those drivers. The edge sits in recognizing that these forecasts assume a system that behaves more smoothly than the real one does. Because copper does not exist as a number — it exists as a chain of physical processes, and those processes do not scale linearly. They stretch, they delay, and eventually, they bottleneck. [...] The easiest way to see this is to stop thinking about copper as supply and start thinking about copper as movement. Production data alone gives a misleading sense of stability. The United States produces just over 1.1 million tonnes annually, Canada contributes roughly 0.5 million tonnes, and at first glance, that suggests a region with meaningful supply capacity. But once you follow the material, the structure looks very different. In 2023, the U.S. still imported approximately 890,000 tonnes of refined copper, while Canada exported around 450,000 tonnes of concentrate, most of it to Asia for processing. This means the system is not self-contained; it is dependent on long-distance logistics and external refining capacity. Copper is mined in one place, processed in another, and consumed in a third. snippet: What makes the current copper setup so interesting is not that the market is wrong, but that it is incomplete in a very specific way. Most participants already understand that demand is going higher, and in fact, that part of the thesis has become consensus. You hear the same numbers repeated across desks: roughly 25 million tonnes of annual demand today, moving toward 35–40 million tonnes over the next decade, driven by electrification, AI infrastructure, renewable energy, and increasingly electrified defense systems. There is no edge in restating those drivers. The edge sits in recognizing that these forecasts assume a system that behaves more smoothly than the real one does. Because copper does not exist as a number — it exists as a chain of physical processes, and those processes do not scale linearly. They stretch, they delay, and eventually, they bottleneck. [...] The easiest way to see this is to stop thinking about copper as supply and start thinking about copper as movement. Production data alone gives a misleading sense of stability. Because copper does not exist as a number — it exists as a chain of physical processes, and those processes do not scale linearly. They stretch, they delay, and eventually, they bottleneck. [...] The easiest way to see this is to stop thinking about copper as supply and start thinking about copper as movement. Production data alone gives a misleading sense of stability. The United States produces just over 1.1 million tonnes annually, Canada contributes roughly 0.5 million tonnes, and at first glance, that suggests a region with meaningful supply capacity. But once you follow the material, the structure looks very different. In 2023, the U.S. still imported approximately 890,000 tonnes of refined copper, while Canada exported around 450,000 tonnes of concentrate, most of it to Asia for processing. snippet: What makes the current copper setup so interesting is not that the market is wrong, but that it is incomplete in a very specific way. Most participants already understand that demand is going higher, and in fact, that part of the thesis has become consensus. You hear the same numbers repeated across desks: roughly 25 million tonnes of annual demand today, moving toward 35–40 million tonnes over the next decade, driven by electrification, AI infrastructure, renewable energy, and increasingly electrified defense systems. There is no edge in restating those drivers. The edge sits in recognizing that these forecasts assume a system that behaves more smoothly than the real one does. Because copper does not exist as a number — it exists as a chain of physical processes, and those processes do not scale linearly. They stretch, they delay, and eventually, they bottleneck. [...] The easiest way to see this is to stop thinking about copper as supply and start thinking about copper as movement. Production data alone gives a misleading sense of stability. The United States produces just over 1.1 million tonnes annually, Canada contributes roughly 0.5 million tonnes, and at first glance, that suggests a region with meaningful supply capacity. But once you follow the material, the structure looks very different. In 2023, the U.S. still imported approximately 890,000 tonnes of refined copper, while Canada exported around 450,000 tonnes of concentrate, most of it to Asia for processing. This means the system is not self-contained; it is dependent on long-distance logistics and external refining capacity. Copper is mined in one place, processed in another, and consumed in a third. snippet: What makes the current copper setup so interesting is not that the market is wrong, but that it is incomplete in a very specific way. You hear the same numbers repeated across desks: roughly 25 million tonnes of annual demand today, moving toward 35–40 million tonnes over the next decade, driven by electrification, AI infrastructure, renewable energy, and increasingly electrified defense systems. There is no edge in restating those drivers. The edge sits in recognizing that these forecasts assume a system that behaves more smoothly than the real one does. Because copper does not exist as a number — it exists as a chain of physical processes, and those processes do not scale linearly. They stretch, they delay, and eventually, they bottleneck. [...] The easiest way to see this is to stop thinking about copper as supply and start thinking about copper as movement. Production data alone gives a misleading sense of stability. But once you follow the material, the structure looks very different. In 2023, the U.S. still imported approximately 890,000 tonnes of refined copper, while Canada exported around 450,000 tonnes of concentrate, most of it to Asia for processing. This means the system is not self-contained; it is dependent on long-distance logistics and external refining capacity. Copper is mined in one place, processed in another, and consumed in a third. snippet: What makes the current copper setup so interesting is not that the market is wrong, but that it is incomplete in a very specific way. Most participants already understand that demand is going higher, and in fact, that part of the thesis has become consensus. You hear the same numbers repeated across desks: roughly 25 million tonnes of annual demand today, moving toward 35–40 million tonnes over the next decade, driven by electrification, AI infrastructure, renewable energy, and increasingly electrified defense systems. There is no edge in restating those drivers. The edge sits in recognizing that these forecasts assume a system that behaves more smoothly than the real one does. Because copper does not exist as a number — it exists as a chain of physical processes, and those processes do not scale linearly. They stretch, they delay, and eventually, they bottleneck. [...] The easiest way to see this is to stop thinking about copper as supply and start thinking about copper as movement. Production data alone gives a misleading sense of stability. The United States produces just over 1.1 million tonnes annually, Canada contributes roughly 0.5 million tonnes, and at first glance, that suggests a region with meaningful supply capacity. But once you follow the material, the structure looks very different. In 2023, the U.S. still imported approximately 890,000 tonnes of refined copper, while Canada exported around 450,000 tonnes of concentrate, most of it to Asia for processing. This means the system is not self-contained; it is dependent on long-distance logistics and external refining capacity. Copper is mined in one place, processed in another, and consumed in a third. snippet: What makes the current copper setup so interesting is not that the market is wrong, but that it is incomplete in a very specific way. Most participants already understand that demand is going higher, and in fact, that part of the thesis has become consensus. You hear the same numbers repeated across desks: roughly 25 million tonnes of annual demand today, moving toward 35–40 million tonnes over the next decade, driven by electrification, AI infrastructure, renewable energy, and increasingly electrified defense systems. There is no edge in restating those drivers. The edge sits in recognizing that these forecasts assume a system that behaves more smoothly than the real one does. Because copper does not exist as a number — it exists as a chain of physical processes, and those processes do not scale linearly. They stretch, they delay, and eventually, they bottleneck. [...] The easiest way to see this is to stop thinking about copper as supply and start thinking about copper as movement. Production data alone gives a misleading sense of stability. The United States produces just over 1.1 million tonnes annually, Canada contributes roughly 0.5 million tonnes, and at first glance, that suggests a region with meaningful supply capacity. But once you follow the material, the structure looks very different. In 2023, the U.S. still imported approximately 890,000 tonnes of refined copper, while Canada exported around 450,000 tonnes of concentrate, most of it to Asia for processing. This means the system is not self-contained; it is dependent on long-distance logistics and external refining capacity. Copper is mined in one place, processed in another, and consumed in a third. You hear the same numbers repeated across desks: roughly 25 million tonnes of annual demand today, moving toward 35–40 million tonnes over the next decade, driven by electrification, AI infrastructure, renewable energy, and increasingly electrified defense systems. There is no edge in restating those drivers. The edge sits in recognizing that these forecasts assume a system that behaves more smoothly than the real one does. Because copper does not exist as a number — it exists as a chain of physical processes, and those processes do not scale linearly. They stretch, they delay, and eventually, they bottleneck. [...] The easiest way to see this is to stop thinking about copper as supply and start thinking about copper as movement. Production data alone gives a misleading sense of stability. The United States produces just over 1.1 million tonnes annually, Canada contributes roughly 0.5 million tonnes, and at first glance, that suggests a region with meaningful supply capacity. But once you follow the material, the structure looks very different. In 2023, the U.S. still imported approximately 890,000 tonnes of refined copper, while Canada exported around 450,000 tonnes of concentrate, most of it to Asia for processing. This means the system is not self-contained; it is dependent on long-distance logistics and external refining capacity. Copper is mined in one place, processed in another, and consumed in a third. snippet: What makes the current copper setup so interesting is not that the market is wrong, but that it is incomplete in a very specific way. Most participants already understand that demand is going higher, and in fact, that part of the thesis has become consensus. You hear the same numbers repeated across desks: roughly 25 million tonnes of annual demand today, moving toward 35–40 million tonnes over the next decade, driven by electrification, AI infrastructure, renewable energy, and increasingly electrified defense systems. There is no edge in restating those drivers. The edge sits in recognizing that these forecasts assume a system that behaves more smoothly than the real one does. Because copper does not exist as a number — it exists as a chain of physical processes, and those processes do not scale linearly. They stretch, they delay, and eventually, they bottleneck. [...] The easiest way to see this is to stop thinking about copper as supply and start thinking about copper as movement. Production data alone gives a misleading sense of stability. The United States produces just over 1.1 million tonnes annually, Canada contributes roughly 0.5 million tonnes, and at first glance, that suggests a region with meaningful supply capacity. But once you follow the material, the structure looks very different. In 2023, the U.S. still imported approximately 890,000 tonnes of refined copper, while Canada exported around 450,000 tonnes of concentrate, most of it to Asia for processing. This means the system is not self-contained; it is dependent on long-distance logistics and external refining capacity. Copper is mined in one place, processed in another, and consumed in a third. That is the top of a multi-megabyte file (Apple's is around 15-20 MB uncompressed, roughly 3-4 MB gzipped; Microsoft's is comparable). The SEC data JSON format is fully documented and freely available for every US public company, but the shape surprises most developers the first time they open it. This post walks through the structure of the SEC XBRL JSON endpoints, how to filter facts by form and period, and what a minimal parsing pipeline looks like in Python. [...] This is Apple' [...] A single company will have hundreds of tags under`us-gaap`, plus a small`dei`(Document and Entity Information) block with metadata like`EntityCommonStockSharesOutstanding`. One useful property of the Company Facts endpoint: it exposes only standardized taxonomies (`us-gaap` and`dei`), not the company-specific extension tags that also exist in the raw XBRL instance document. Those custom tags, which are not comparable across companies, are filtered out of this view by design. [...] Revenue is always`USD` for US filers. Diluted EPS appears under`USD/shares`(the SEC writes this as`USD-per-shares` in some documentation). Share counts appear under`shares`. [...] 1. When aggregating monetary fields, filter to`USD` only. If a foreign filer reports in CAD or EUR, those facts live in their own unit key and should not be added to USD totals without conversion. 2. Share counts and EPS use different unit keys than dollar values. A pipeline that only looks at`USD` will silently skip EPS and shares outstanding. Specifically, we use textual analysis of earnings calls from the S&P Global Market Intelligence database, which includes 5,000-7,500 earnings calls from U.S. and foreign firms per quarter, to construct firm sentiment indexes about the bottlenecks. The benefit of this approach is that we have very timely data to synthesize information about what firms are seeing on the ground and what challenges they face. Those custom tags, which are not comparable across companies, are filtered out of this view by design. [...] Revenue is always`USD` for US filers.
